1:
Delitzsch states the psalm's argument in a sentence: do not let the prosperity of the ungodly vex you, but wait, since it will suddenly end and the issue decides between righteous and unrighteous. He notes the epithets it has attracted — a mirror of providence, a medicine against murmuring, the garment of the pious inscribed here is the patience of the saints — and observes that the thought comes not in ordinary strophes but in short proverbial utterances following the alphabet, with deliberate repetitions to press it deeper. Calvin puts the difficulty more sharply. The bolder a man's contempt of God, the happier he seems to live; and since prosperity looks like a token of favour, one might conclude either that the world is governed by chance or that God makes no difference between good and bad. The psalm's answer is paradoxical and repugnant to human reason: the felicity of the wicked is transient and cursed, while God's servants never cease to be happy even in their greatest calamities. That, Calvin says, is why the doctrine is profitable — it withdraws the mind from the present aspect of things until God calls the ungodly to account as thieves who have abused his bounty.

Clarke doubts the ascription. The title gives the psalm to David and most versions follow, but he thinks it more likely a consoling ode for the captives in Babylon, who had every temptation to envy when idolaters prospered while the worshippers of the true God lived in slavery; he counts the return predicted in no fewer than ten places. He describes the acrostic — two verses under each letter, only the first showing it — and lists its irregularities, three letters having lost a hemistich apiece. Ellicott works the vocabulary. The verb behind fret means to heat or inflame oneself and occurs elsewhere only in Proverbs; the word for envy has a similar root, so the two stand in close parallelism, much as we speak of burning with jealousy. He notes that the alphabetic structure lets the poet mount a threefold exhortation — trust, commit, rest — and that the grass metaphor, elsewhere a mournful sigh over human weakness applied without distinction of good or bad, becomes here a comfort to the godly. Gill and Wesley keep it simple: the prosperity is short-lived, and the saints may be grieved at evildoers without the undue warmth the verb itself warns against.

Henry begins with the psalmist rather than the wicked. David preaches this to himself first, communing upon his bed, to suppress the corrupt passions he found working there, and only then leaves it in writing for others — and that is preached best which is first preached to ourselves. He traces the temptation in stages: looking abroad we see the world full of men who flourish and do what they will; looking within we fret at God as unkind to his church, envy the liberty of those who get wealth unlawfully, and think them the only happy people. Fretfulness and envy, he adds, are their own punishment: the uneasiness of the spirit, the rottenness of the bones. Spurgeon supplies the images: nature kindles a fire of jealousy when it sees law-breakers riding on horses and obedient subjects walking in the mire, and it seems hard that the best meat should go to the dogs while loving children pine. But who envies the fat bullock its garlands as it is led to the shambles? On the cure he is brisk — faith cures fretting, since sight is cross-eyed and sees only how things seem, while faith has clearer optics; and true faith is actively obedient, there being a joy in holy activity that drives off the rust of discontent. Augustine alone opens somewhere else entirely, on the day whose hour God willed to stay unknown so the heart might always be ready for what it knows must come.
4:
Spurgeon reads these verses as a rising staircase. The man first told not to fret was next commanded to trust, and is now told to delight; the counsel he draws is odd but exact — in a certain sense imitate the wicked, for they delight in their portion, so take care to delight in yours, and instead of envying them you will pity them. Every name, attribute and deed of God should be delightful, the soul meditating on them as glad as an epicure with a relish for his dainties. On the promise he is careful: the innermost desires are meant, not casual wishes, and it is safe to give such men a free hand because their will is already subdued to God's. Clarke reaches the same limit by a shorter road — the godly man never indulges a desire he cannot form into a prayer — and takes delighting to mean expecting all one's happiness from God. Gill spreads it wider: the persons of God, his perfections, his works, his word and his people.

The next precept is a picture, and the readers draw it differently. Clarke takes the verb as rolling a load, from the camel that kneels until its burden is rolled onto it. Delitzsch presses the surrender further: roll the cares of your life's way onto God, leave its guidance entirely to him, doing nothing yourself, and he will accomplish it gloriously — the Greek, he notes, mistranslated the verb as uncover. Gill will not go that far. He records the alternatives, reveal thy way and roll thy way, explains that revealing is not for God's information, since it is our duty to ask and his delight to hear, and insists the command does not mean men should sit still and leave everything to be done for them. They are to seek direction and strength for every business, and give God the glory without trusting anything of their own. Wesley reduces it to commending one's cares by fervent prayer, Spurgeon to a medicine for envy: the ploughman sows and harrows and leaves the harvest to God, since he cannot cover the heavens with clouds or command the rain.

On the vindication there is agreement. Delitzsch has misjudged righteousness brought to light like the sun breaking through darkness and down-trodden right like the brightness of noon, an image Ellicott traces to an Eastern dawn climbing to meridian glory; Clarke makes it instantaneous, God saying let thy innocence appear as once he said let there be light. The last precept divides them over how much silence is meant. Clarke renders it be silent, be dumb — do not find fault with thy Maker — and reads the second verb, being reflexive, as setting oneself to expect God. Ellicott gives it as Hush! Be still! Delitzsch defines the first verb as resignation, a quiet of mind resting on God and renouncing self-help, and the second as an inward gathering of oneself in hope. But Gill guards the command from misuse: it does not mean a stupid indolence or a stoical apathy, as though we were sticks and stones without concern under God's hand, nor an entire silence under affliction, since we may own it as his, pray to have it sanctified, and tell others what goodness we found in it. What it excludes is arraigning and murmuring. Henry says the same — a submissive silence, not a sullen one — and adds that patient bearing with patient expectation is as much our interest as our duty, and that when the heart begins to rise a man should stroke down his folly. Spurgeon closes on the waiting: time is nothing to God, let it be nothing to you; in a story we wait for the end to clear the plot, and there is more of the love of God in your defeats than in the successes of the wicked.
8:
Anger is the dangerous stage. Spurgeon calls anger anywhere madness and here aggravated insanity, and warns that fretfulness lies on the verge of great sin: many who indulged a murmuring disposition came at last to sin outright to gain their fancied rights. Ellicott sharpens the clause to only evil can come of it, and Delitzsch reads it as standing alone — the fretting ends in your involving yourself in sin, while the men you make yourself like by such murmuring will be cut off. It is the end, he says, the final and consequently eternal end, that decides the matter. Wesley states the caution briefly: if grief arises, take care it does not transport you to sin.

The promise attached to meekness is where the readers part company. Clarke insists the word rendered earth should be land throughout the psalm and means Judea, so the meek are the afflicted Jewish captives and the verse promises their return to the inheritance given their fathers. Ellicott also translates heirs of the land and takes it of Canaan, but adds that the Beatitude widens the promise: the contented servant of God gets more true blessedness out of the earth, and so more truly possesses it, than the ungodly who are lords of broad acres. Delitzsch goes further, noting the words in the mouth of the Preacher on the Mount and concluding that meekness content with God will at length inherit the land, yea the earth — whatever self-love amasses falling at last to the meek. Wesley thinks it was largely fulfilled in the church's state then, and reads the peace promised with it as partly outward prosperity but principally the inward peace of God's favour.

The disappearance of the wicked is read narrowly or widely. Gill will not allow annihilation: non-entities have no being anywhere, and these men die, rise at the last day and stand before the judgment seat; what ceases is their flourishing presence in the world. Ellicott keeps it social: he has dropped out of his place, and his tribe knows him no more. Clarke makes it a dated prophecy, the fall of Babylon, an empire then in its splendour which the captives lived to see so completely overturned that its site can no longer be identified. On the plotting, Spurgeon asks why the wicked cannot let the good man alone and answers from the enmity between the two seeds, and why he plots rather than fights fairly and answers from the subtlety of the serpent; if they cannot gnaw they will gnash, and if they may not bite they will bark. Delitzsch adds that the gnashing is anger rather than mockery, and that God treats an assault on the righteous as an assault on himself, laughing at the schemer because he already sees his day. On the weapons drawn, Delitzsch puts the emphasis on the possessive: they perish by their own weapon — which Ellicott calls the law of retaliation and Gill illustrates from the death of Saul.

The closing proverb is admired by everyone. Spurgeon hears in the original an allusion to the noise of a multitude — the hurly-burly of riotous wealth against the quiet of a humbler portion. Content, he says, finds much in little, while for a wicked heart the whole world is too little. Delitzsch confirms it, the word being a noisy crowd applied to earthly possessions, and marks the contrast of one righteous man with many unrighteous. Ellicott supplies the reasons: great riches bring corresponding cares and often lead to ruinous indulgence, and contentment seldom dwells with the mammon of unrighteousness. Clarke puts it as a maxim: whatever a good man has, has God's blessing in it, while even the blessings of the wicked are cursed. Gill concedes the fact behind the proverb, that though some of the righteous have been rich, generally the wicked hold the larger share.
17:
The broken arms are read as capacity lost. Ellicott points out that the arms meant are limbs of the body, not the sword and bow of the previous verse, the contrast being with the arms of God under the righteous. Delitzsch puts it plainly: a man whose arms are broken can neither injure others nor help himself, whereas God himself upholds the other party. Clarke reads it as power to do evil withdrawn, talents lent and abused being resumed; Gill divides it between the sword arm that cannot strike and the substance in which the wicked trusted. Spurgeon coins the phrase the others circle: God often makes implacable men incapable men — and what is more contemptible than toothless malice? On the knowing that follows, Gill says God knows not only how long they will live but the nature of their days; Clarke has him acquainted with each man's sufferings and ability to bear them, so that he will either shorten the trial or increase the strength.

Delitzsch takes the verse further, then stops short as none of the others do. The life of those who love God is, with all its vicissitudes, an object of his providential care, and he suffers his own neither to lose their heritage nor to be lost to it. But the everlasting inheritance here, he insists, is not yet conceived as reaching into the future world as in the New Testament, and surviving the famine refers only to this present life. Wesley reads the same words the other way: the inheritance passes to them and their seed for ever, and at death is exchanged for one infinitely better. Gill takes the perishing set against it as eternal perdition, not the death common to good and bad. Clarke keeps his exilic frame and hears another indirect assurance of restoration; on the freedom from shame, their enemies will never be able to say they trusted their God and were beaten for it.

The comparison drawn for God's enemies is the hardest phrase here. Clarke says the verse has troubled the critics, reports the versions reading it as vanishing like smoke as soon as they are exalted to honour, then follows the Hebrew: as sacrificial fat is wholly consumed on the altar, so shall they consume away in the fire of God's wrath. Ellicott replies that it is now generally allowed the words should be rendered as the glory of the meadows, returning the psalm to the grass of its second verse. Delitzsch notes the play of sound in the original and finds both senses admissible — that they are resolved into smoke, or go as smoke goes, thick at first and thinner until it is not there.

The last verse sets an unpaid debt against an open hand, and the readers divide: vice, or punishment? Gill takes it as disposition, not incapacity: they do not pay because they will not, having taken no thought of it when they borrowed. Henry begins in the same place — it is not merely a shameful paltry thing but a sinful wicked thing not to repay what we have borrowed — then reports the other reading fairly, that some make this an instance not of wickedness but of the misery to which judgment reduces them, forced to borrow and then unable to repay. Both, he concludes, are to be feared: a great sin in those able to deny their debts, a great misery in those unable to pay. Clarke holds both at once, the wicked man obliged to become debtor to those he once despised, refusing because he is wicked or failing because beggared; and he grounds the contrast in grace, mercy shown because mercy was received. Delitzsch reads the pair as an old promise in proverbial form, the downfall of one and the easier charity of the other being curse and blessing already spoken.
22:
Whose steps are ordered is disputed from the word up. Clarke observes that nothing answers to good in the text: the noun means a strong man or hero, used to show that even the most powerful must be upheld or his strength will avail little. Ellicott reads it generally, on the strength of parallel proverbs: man's steps are established by Jehovah, all stability in human conduct coming from his guidance. Delitzsch insists on the verb: the steps are made firm, not ordered or directed as the Greek and Latin have it; and the noun means man in an ethical sense, so the line says more than the proverb that man proposes and God disposes. Gill keeps it to the man already blessed, whose good conduct is not of himself; Wesley has him established so that he shall not fall into mischief.

The fall in the next verse is read two ways. Gill takes it of falling into temptation and by it into sins, and great ones. Clarke denies it: neither the text nor any version intimates a fall into sin, but into trouble. One ancient version, he notes, renders it though he should fall into sickness he shall not die; and a man may lie under his adversaries for a time, as the Jews did under the captivity, without being forsaken.

Then comes the psalm's most awkward line, answered with unusual candour. Clarke takes it as literally true in all cases: he is grey-headed himself, has conversed with religious people in every situation of life, and has not to his knowledge seen one instance to the contrary. Spurgeon will not say the same. It is not my observation just as it stands, he writes, having relieved the children of undoubtedly good men who came to him as common mendicants — though this casts no doubt on the psalmist, whose dispensation was more outward. He narrows the claim: that the righteous are never forsaken is a rule without exception, while that their children never beg is seldom broken, and usually through the sons' idleness. Count the children of godly parents in the workhouse, he says, and again in the gaol. Wesley makes it doctrinal: the temporal promises were more express to the Jews than to Christians. Delitzsch reaches for an old rule, that bodily promises are understood with the exception of the cross and chastisement, and concedes that the psalm does not deny temporary forsakenness. It was written to meet that doubt, and meets it by setting what abides against what is transitory — without, he adds, knowledge of any final adjustment in a future world, so its problem is solved only in the light of the New Testament.

The exhortation returns at the end, and Spurgeon calls its two halves the quintessence of the psalm: as Lot left Sodom without a backward look, so sin is to be left, no truce held with it, and the man who neglects to do good will soon fall into evil. Clarke finds the twofold gift of grace, strength to overcome evil and to do right, and hears another assurance of residence in the land. Delitzsch notes that the imperative keeps its force while carrying a promise; Wesley extends it beyond the land to heaven. The verse after is textually broken, and both technicians say so. Ellicott reports that the stanza which should begin with one letter of the alphabet is missing from the Hebrew, that a slight change agreeing with the Greek and Latin restores it as the unjust shall be punished, and that a transcriber was misled by a similar letter nearby. Delitzsch adds that the verse division is wrong, and the extra line in the Greek an ancient attempt at the same repair. Clarke reads the closing threat as a family matter: children who follow wicked parents are cut off like them, judgments descending to posterity as well as mercies.
30:
Spurgeon explains why the psalm turns to speech here. A poem devoted to the different fates of just and wicked needs a test by which the two can be told apart, and a man's tongue is no ill index of his character — the mouth betrays the heart. The righteous man's talk gives an honest verdict on things and men; it is neither ribald nor profane, and our conversation is of far more consequence than some men imagine. Righteousness, he adds, is wisdom in action. Clarke says it negatively: foolish and corrupt conversation cannot come out of such a mouth. Gill reads the verb as meditating rather than speaking, so what is uttered has first been turned over: the wisdom of God in creation and grace, Christ who is wisdom itself, and the gospel, ancient wisdom ordained before the world.

The heart supplying the mouth is described three ways. Gill takes it as the moral law, written in Adam at creation and greatly obliterated by sin, of which remains persist even among those who never had it; in regeneration it is reinscribed, and the man knows its spirituality, the impossibility of justification by it, and Christ as its fulfilling end. Clarke reads it as the promised new covenant already fulfilled, the precepts written not only in his Bible but in his heart, so that the heart dictates to his eyes, mouth, hands and feet. Delitzsch states a principle about moral stability: the walk of the righteous has a fixed inward rule, the law being no external object of knowledge or compulsory precept but something in the heart, joined — since it is the law of the God he loves — to his will as the motive of what he does. Spurgeon compresses it — the best thing in the best place, producing the best results. Wesley adds that the sliding warned against is swerving from the rule, and that the psalmist, having shown God's care over the righteous, is now giving their character.

Watching and judging come next. Gill has the wicked observing every step, waiting for the righteous man to halt, and God delivering him in his own time. Delitzsch sets God's examination against that of men: if men judge the righteous, the supreme Judge does not condemn but acquits — and he recalls an early writer's cry to his fellow-sufferers that condemnation by the world is absolution before God.

The final precept is waiting, defined so as to exclude idleness. Clarke insists this is the true mode of waiting Scripture recommends — keeping God's way, using his ordinances, living in obedience — and finds the picture in the verb, a straight line drawn from the human heart, along its intense desire, to God. Gill agrees, waiting in the way of his appointments, where the design of his providences and the end of the wicked can be learned. Henry divides the labour: duty is ours, so we must keep God's way and never turn out of it nor loiter in it, while events are God's, so we attend the motions of providence — and God is a good Master to his working servants and his waiting servants alike. Spurgeon calls waiting a lofty eminence, easy to say and hard to do: in obedience as a servant, in hope as an heir, in expectation as a believer. Over the promise attached they separate. Clarke keeps his exilic reading, the exaltation lifting the captives to the land of their fathers and the seeing fulfilled when they watched the Babylonian empire destroyed. Delitzsch takes it as possession of the land from which the evildoers, who carried themselves as its sole lords, are now cut off. Spurgeon widens it to all earthly good that is really good and heavenly good without stint, and turns the last clause into a rebuke for fretfulness and an incentive to gratitude.
35:
The tree the wicked man is likened to has never been identified. Ellicott notes the Hebrew word elsewhere means a native as against a foreigner, so an indigenous tree is meant; he doubts any species is intended, but if one is it must be an evergreen — possibly the sweet bay. Delitzsch takes it for an oak or terebinth standing in its native soil from time immemorial, grown to a gigantic stem with a wide overhanging head. Both note that the Greek and Latin, altering the text slightly, read cedars of Lebanon; neither accepts it. Clarke looks past botany and asks whether the picture is not the great tree of Nebuchadnezzar's vision. Gill will not name a man but is sure one is meant — someone in great authority, as Haman was in the Persian court, formidable and terrible. Spurgeon reads the verse as a diary entry, and thinks it well if we too took notes of providences: the man added house to house and field to field, ever verdant like a laurel.

What happens next is disputed grammatically. Gill has the man pass away on a sudden, his riches coming to nothing or his soul required of him in the midst of prosperity; the bay tree, he adds, very quickly grows old. Wesley says he was gone in an instant, with no monument or remainder of him left. Clarke identifies the moment as the fall of Babylon. Delitzsch objects that the verb cannot mean he vanished away, since that will not suit a tree, and renders it that one passed by — a spectator went past and the growth was gone. Ellicott construes it the same way, noting that the Greek and Latin lighten the difficulty by making the psalmist the one who passes.

The verse that follows is the psalm's hardest, and two readers call the familiar rendering wrong. Ellicott declares it quite wrongly translated, since the noun must mean posterity, and says the parallelism decides it: a posterity shall be to the man of peace, while the posterity of the wicked is destroyed. Clarke reaches the same verdict from the versions, which he says render it preserve innocence and keep equity in view, for the man of peace shall leave a numerous posterity; the original cannot possibly bear the received translation. Delitzsch reads it the same way: the man of peace has a future in his posterity, the apostates blotted out so completely that no posterity remains to carry their name. Wesley alone keeps the traditional sense: though such a man meet troubles on his way, all shall end well.

Over the word perfect Gill mounts a refusal. None are perfect in themselves, he says, not the most holy man on earth: grace is implanted whole in regeneration but opens gradually, sin remains in the best of men, and no saint ever claimed perfection. There is a perfection of parts though not of degrees, the new man being formed in all his parts before any is grown; and since the word often denotes sincerity, those who received grace in truth may be called perfect. On the destruction set against it he restricts the word to obstinate transgressors who live and die in their sins, since all men are transgressors in Adam; Wesley reads it as all without exception, and Henry adds that nothing can be well which will end ill. The close belongs to the salvation. Delitzsch notes that coming from God it is sure and enduring, and that the word usually rendered strength means here not a fortress but a hiding-place. Clarke grounds it in the God who made them righteous by blotting out their sins, and takes the last clause practically: they keep faith and obedience in exercise, and he continues to save them. Gill ends where the psalm does, with a salvation of God only and entire — to the uttermost, from all sin.
